title: Error Propagation & Significant Figures Rules
notes: Significant figures show how precise a measurement is. In 0.00450 m the figures that count are 4, 5 and the trailing zero; the zeros before 4 only locate the decimal point.
For multiplication or division, round the final result to the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs. For addition or subtraction, round to the least precise decimal place.
Worked case: 2.34×1.2 equals 2.808 and rounds to 2.8, because 1.2 has two significant figures. The sum 12.11+0.3 equals 12.41 and rounds to 12.4, because 0.3 is known only to tenths.
Keep guard digits through intermediate steps and round once at the end. Exact counts and defined conversion factors, such as 1 m = 100 cm, do not limit the significant figures of a result.
Relative uncertainty scales with a power. If A=πr² and r is uncertain by 1%, A is uncertain by about 2%, because the power 2 doubles the relative uncertainty before the final rounding.

Significant figures show the precision you actually have. In 0.00450 the significant figures are 4, 5 and the last 0. When you multiply, the result should carry no more significant figures than the less precise factor. When you add, you line up the decimal places instead.
confusion: Do not apply the fewest-significant-figures rule to addition.
Exact counted values do not impose measurement precision.
A symbol is not a number until the unit is named.
A proportional relation is not an equality until the constant is included.
A vector answer needs a direction as well as a magnitude.
A special case, such as a right angle or a steady temperature, has to be stated before it is used.
